standard.title: Plan Valid, Reproducible Investigations
standard.description: plan and conduct valid, reproducible investigations to answer questions and test hypotheses, including identifying and controlling for possible sources of error and, as appropriate, developing and following risk assessments, considering ethical issues, and addressing key considerations regarding heritage sites and artefacts on Country/Place
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can plan and conduct investigations to test predictions, identifying variables and describing methods (AC9S7I02). They have not yet explicitly focused on validity and reproducibility as criteria for method quality, or systematically identified and controlled sources of error as part of planning.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students plan and conduct investigations that are valid (method measures what it claims to measure, variables controlled) and reproducible (method can be repeated by others to get consistent results) — systematically identifying sources of error and explaining how they are controlled. Students can develop and follow risk assessments, consider ethical issues in investigation design, and recognise responsibilities regarding heritage sites and artefacts on Country/Place.

nodes.label: Validity and reproducibility as method criteria
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain what validity and reproducibility mean as criteria for a scientific investigation method, and identify whether a described method satisfies each criterion.
nodes.minimum_width: Define validity (the method measures what it claims to measure) and reproducibility (the method can be repeated by others to obtain consistent results), and apply one criterion to evaluate a described method.
nodes.typical_width: Define both validity and reproducibility, explain why each matters for scientific investigation, and evaluate a described method against both criteria — identifying specific features of the method that support or undermine each.
wider: Determine the reproducibility of a specific field investigation design — e.g. a survey of traffic passing a school — examining what features of the method determine whether another person running it would get the same result.

Distinguish internal validity (are the results due to the independent variable, not something else?) from external validity (can the results be generalised?) as two dimensions of validity relevant at Year 9.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who treat validity and reproducibility as generic 'good science' terms without specific meaning cannot systematically identify sources of error (Node 2) or evaluate their own method quality. These criteria are the framework for all subsequent investigation planning — without them, error identification becomes arbitrary.

response_modes.reason: Validity and reproducibility need to be operationalised as questions students ask of a method: 'Is the measurement capturing what we want to measure, or is it capturing something else?' and 'If someone else ran this, what might they do differently that would produce a different result?' These question structures need explicit modelling.

success_criteria: Can define validity and reproducibility with precision — not just 'it works' and 'you can do it again'.
Can identify a specific feature of a method that threatens validity or reproducibility.
Does not conflate the two criteria — can explain how a method could be reproducible but not valid.

nodes.label: Identifying and controlling sources of error
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify possible sources of error in an investigation method and explain how controlling or accounting for each error source increases validity and reproducibility.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two sources of error in a described or planned investigation and explain how each could be controlled or reduced.
nodes.typical_width: Systematically identify multiple sources of error across measurement, procedure and environmental factors, and describe specific control strategies for each — distinguishing between errors that can be eliminated and those that must be minimised and acknowledged.
wider: Examine the difference between random error (varies unpredictably) and systematic error (consistently biased in one direction), and explain how each affects data quality differently — connecting to AC9S9I06 (assessing validity of methods).

Identify possible sources of error in a method and examine whether further testing or extra variable control is needed — applying the principle that error identification should drive method refinement, not just documentation.
success_criteria: Can identify at least two sources of error with specific explanations — not generic 'human error'.
Can describe a specific control strategy for each identified error source.
Can explain how uncontrolled error affects the validity of conclusions.

nodes.label: Risk assessment, ethics and Country/Place considerations
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify potential hazards in an investigation, develop a risk assessment, consider ethical issues relevant to the investigation context, and describe responsibilities regarding heritage sites and artefacts on Country/Place.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least one hazard in a described investigation, describe how it would be addressed in a risk assessment, and identify one ethical consideration relevant to a described investigation type.
nodes.typical_width: Develop a risk assessment for a planned investigation (identifying hazard, likelihood, severity, and control measure), consider ethical issues relevant to the investigation (animal use, participant welfare, cultural sensitivity), and explain responsibilities regarding heritage sites when conducting field investigations.
wider: Examine ethical guidelines for animal use in scientific investigations — understanding the framework that governs care and use of animals for scientific purposes before planning any investigation involving animals.

Examine First Nations Australians' heritage laws and the public responsibility to report new sites or artefacts — describing the consequences for disturbing heritage sites on, above or below the land surface, or in waters, when planning field investigations.
success_criteria: Can identify at least one investigation hazard and describe a control measure.
Can identify at least one ethical consideration relevant to a described investigation.
Can describe responsibilities regarding heritage sites in field investigation contexts.
